script: [serious] In the summer of 1917, two girls came home from a stream in Yorkshire with a photograph. In it, a nine-year-old girl looks straight at the camera. And in front of her, dancing in the air, are four tiny winged figures. Fairies. Within a few years, that photograph had been studied by photography experts, printed in one of the most famous magazines in Britain, and championed by one of the most famous writers in the world, the man who created Sherlock Holmes. Many people believed it. And for more than sixty years, the two girls who took it never told anyone the truth. This is the complete case file on the Cottingley Fairies. Let's open it. The village of Cottingley sits near Bradford, in West Yorkshire. In 1917, Frances Griffiths, aged nine, had just arrived from South Africa with her mother, to live with her aunt's family, the Wrights. Her cousin, Elsie Wright, was sixteen. Elsie was a gifted artist. Behind the Wrights' house ran a small stream, called a beck, and a wooded glen, where the two girls spent hours playing. The girls said there were fairies down by the beck. The adults did not take it seriously. So one day, Elsie borrowed her father's camera, a small plate camera, and the two girls went down to the stream to prove it. Elsie's father, Arthur Wright, was an amateur photographer with his own darkroom. When he developed the plate that evening, he saw Frances, behind a bush, with four small figures dancing in front of her, one of them playing a pipe. Arthur did not believe it for a second. He knew his daughter could draw. He thought the figures were cut-outs. A couple of months later, the girls came back with a second picture. This time, Elsie sat on the grass, reaching out to a small, winged gnome. Arthur still thought it was a prank, and he remained convinced his daughter had made the figures herself. But Elsie's mother, Polly, was not so sure. And that is where the story could have ended, as a family joke in a house in Yorkshire, if Polly had not been interested in something called Theosophy. Theosophy was a spiritual movement that took the idea of invisible beings, including nature spirits, very seriously. Around 1919, Polly Wright went to a Theosophical Society lecture in Bradford. The subject of the lecture was fairy life. Afterwards, she mentioned her daughter's photographs. They reached Edward Gardner, a leading member of the society, who soon began using them in his lectures. Gardner wanted them checked first. He sent the negatives to a photography expert, Harold Snelling. Snelling's verdict was that the negatives showed no sign of tampering, and were genuine records of whatever had been in front of the camera. The photography company Kodak also examined them. Its technicians found no evidence of faking either. But they would not certify that the photographs were genuine. Those careful words would be repeated, and misunderstood, for decades. And then the photographs reached Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. By then, Doyle was not only the creator of Sherlock Holmes. He was also a committed spiritualist, who had come to believe in life after death during the First World War. He was writing an article about fairies when he heard about Cottingley. In 1920, Edward Gardner travelled to Cottingley himself. He met the family, decided they were honest, and gave each girl a camera and fresh photographic plates. The girls produced three more photographs. One showed Frances with a leaping fairy. One showed Elsie being offered a flower by a fairy. And the fifth, the strangest of all, showed shapes in the long grass that Gardner believed was a kind of fairy sunbath. That same year, Doyle published the photographs in The Strand Magazine, the magazine that had made Sherlock Holmes famous. He presented them as evidence that fairies were real. He later wrote a whole book about it, called The Coming of the Fairies. Some readers were thrilled. Many laughed. But Doyle never changed his mind. A year later, a clairvoyant named Geoffrey Hodson visited the glen with the girls, and claimed that he could see fairies too. The girls later said they had simply humoured him. Doyle died in 1930, still believing. He never learned the truth. After Doyle's book, the excitement faded. The girls took no more fairy photographs. They grew up, married, and moved on with their lives. But the questions never quite went away. In the 1960s and 1970s, reporters tracked them down. In interviews, the cousins stayed careful. Elsie hinted that the fairies were figments of her imagination, but neither woman said outright that the photographs were faked. Then, in 1978, investigators noticed something. The fairies in the first photograph looked almost exactly like an illustration in a children's book from 1914, called Princess Mary's Gift Book. The poses were strikingly similar. Elsie had copied the figures, and added wings. That same year, the skeptic James Randi and a team of investigators analysed the photographs with computer enhancement, and argued that they could see signs of how the figures had been held in place. In the early 1980s, the editor of the British Journal of Photography, Geoffrey Crawley, published his own long investigation, and concluded the photographs were fakes. The two women, now in their seventies and eighties, were running out of room. The evidence was piling up, and the reporters kept calling. In 1983, more than sixty years after the first photograph, the cousins finally admitted it. Elsie had copied the fairies from the book, drawn them on card, cut them out, and stood them up in the grass with hatpins. Once they had fooled Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, Elsie later said, they felt they had to keep quiet. They were two village girls, and he was a famous man. But there was one last twist. Frances agreed that the first four photographs were fakes. But she insisted, until the end of her life, that the fifth one, the strange sunbath picture in the long grass, was real. Elsie said that it was faked too. So what does the Cottingley file really tell us? Not that people a century ago were foolish. The experts were asked whether the photographs had been tampered with, and they answered honestly. They had not been. The fairies really were in front of the camera. They were just made of paper. That is the trap at the heart of this case. A photograph can prove that something was in front of the lens. It cannot tell you what that something was. The experts answered the narrow question they were asked, and the believers heard the answer to a much bigger one. What turned a teenage prank into a sensation was something else. People who wanted to believe, and a famous name who gave them permission to. Two girls tried to prove a story to their parents, and lost control of it. Edward Gardner had sold prints of the photographs at his lectures. Doyle had staked his reputation on them. Each new believer made it harder for two young women to say, it was only a game. And the fifth photograph is still argued about today. So, do you think Frances was telling the truth about the last one? Tell me in the comments. This is Dossier Decoded. Case file: The Cottingley Fairies. Confessed. Almost.
